source.title: Athletic groin pain (part 1): a prospective anatomical diagnosis of 382 patients—clinical findings, MRI findings and patient-reported outcome measures at baseline

paper.citation: Falvey, É. C., King, E., Kinsella, S., & Franklyn-Miller, A. (2016). Athletic groin pain (part 1): A prospective anatomical diagnosis of 382 patients—clinical findings, MRI findings and patient-reported outcome measures at baseline. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 50(7), 423–430. https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2015-094912
paper.abstract: What clinical, MRI, and patient-reported findings characterize athletes presenting with groin pain, and how well do commonly used examination and imaging findings support anatomical diagnostic groupings? The cohort comprised 382 consecutive male patients presenting to secondary or tertiary sports-medicine care with athletic groin pain; mean age was 27.6 years and median symptom duration was 36 weeks (IQR 16–75). Most participants played field-based ball sports, principally Gaelic football, hurling, soccer, and rugby; 25.7% competed at elite and 65.2% at club level. This was a symptomatic referral cohort, not a screening sample of asymptomatic athletes. Prospective descriptive cohort with a standardized history and physical examination performed by two consultant sports physicians and a senior physiotherapist. Examination included hip range of motion and provocation tests, adductor squeeze tests at 90°, 45°, and 0°, pelvic-ring load tests, neurological tension tests, and targeted palpation. All participants underwent MRI reviewed clinically by a sports physician and subsequently reported by a consultant radiologist; diagnostic groupings combined history, examination, and MRI findings. Participants completed the Copenhagen Hip and Groin Outcome Score at presentation.
paper.tldr: This study informs clinical reasoning about athletic groin pain by describing how standardized examination and MRI findings aligned in a large consecutive male referral cohort. Pubic aponeurosis injury was the primary clinical diagnosis in 240 of 382 cases (62.8%), followed by hip injury in 81 (21.2%) and adductor injury in 56 (14.7%). Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Prospective descriptive cohort with a standardized history and physical examination performed by two consultant sports physicians and a senior physiotherapist. Examination included hip range of motion and provocation tests, adductor squeeze tests at 90°, 45°, and 0°, pelvic-ring load tests, neurological tension tests, and targeted palpation. All participants underwent MRI reviewed clinically by a sports physician and subsequently reported by a consultant radiologist; diagnostic groupings combined history, examination, and MRI findings. Participants completed the Copenhagen Hip and Groin Outcome Score at presentation.
paper.findings: Pubic aponeurosis injury was the primary clinical diagnosis in 240 of 382 cases (62.8%), followed by hip injury in 81 (21.2%) and adductor injury in 56 (14.7%). Pain occurred during the 90° adductor squeeze test in 314 cases (82.2%), but squeeze-test findings were not associated with a physician diagnosis of adductor injury; the test appeared sensitive to anterior-groin distress rather than anatomically specific. MRI showed pubic bone marrow oedema in 259 cases (67.8%), abnormal pubic-aponeurosis findings in 201 (52.6%), and abnormal hip findings in 170 (44.5%); only 27 participants (7.1%) had no abnormal MRI finding. Multiple MRI abnormalities were common: 131 participants (34.3%) had two abnormal findings and 112 (29.3%) had three or more. Bone marrow oedema was associated with the diagnosis of pubic-aponeurosis injury in adjusted analyses, but the association attenuated when symptom duration was added.
paper.limitations: The MRI protocol was directed mainly toward anterior-groin soft tissue and omitted axial-oblique femoral head/neck images; clinically indicated hip imaging was obtained separately. Inter-tester reliability of the standardized examination was not assessed. No asymptomatic control group was included, so chronic incidental MRI abnormalities may have contributed to the observed imaging prevalence. Diagnostic categories were produced from the same clinical and imaging information being evaluated; this study describes associations and diagnostic patterns rather than validating a treatment algorithm or independent gold standard. The all-male, largely Gaelic-football/club referral population limits direct transfer to female athletes, adolescents, different sports, and acute presentations.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the adductor squeeze test as a broad pain-provocation and load-tolerance signal, not as a structure-specific diagnosis. In persistent groin pain, combine history, targeted examination, and clinically appropriate imaging while expecting coexisting abnormalities. Do not allow an isolated MRI change or squeeze-test response to dictate rehabilitation without confirming symptom behavior and functional relevance.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, use the adductor squeeze test as a broad pain-provocation and load-tolerance signal, not as a structure-specific diagnosis. In persistent groin pain, combine history, targeted examination, and clinically appropriate imaging while expecting coexisting abnormalities. Do not allow an isolated MRI change or squeeze-test response to dictate rehabilitation without confirming symptom behavior and functional relevance. This study alone does not establish clearance criteria or a complete return-to-sport progression.
